reason: A cupule (cupule bearer) can be cup-shaped, as in 'shallowly cupular'. Some examples just repeat the part name, but the pair is meaningful.
Seeds can be woolly (lanate), as in the Salix and Epilobium type of hairy seed.
The costa (moss midrib) can be rough, for example roughened at the back.
An orchid labellum can be fleshy. The 'fleshy callus' example is a part of the labellum, but the pair is still fine.
A floral disc can be conical.
Paraphyllia (moss stem outgrowths) can be present or absent. This fits the absence pattern.
Wrong reading. A spurred stipule has a spur as a part, and the stipule itself is not spur-shaped. It belongs to has-part spur, and the spur length belongs to the spur.
A primary vein can be pubescent. The examples are annotated correctly.
Secondary veins can be prominent or inconspicuous on a leaf face.

Petiolate versus subsessile cotyledons is a real contrast, but the attribute is too vague. The examples also include a petiole length, which belongs to the petiole. A rule would need to map 'petiolate/sessile' to a value term and send lengths to the petiole.
An androphore can be hairy. The examples are acceptable, though the stellate hairs may sit on a neighbouring part.
Wrong part. 'Entire at base' means the margin is entire in the basal part. The quality belongs to the leaf margin, not to the lamina base.
PATO irregular spatial pattern is a different meaning from 'irregular in shape'. The examples also mix in irregular splitting and surface. A rule would have to map irregular shape to a shape term.
A pyrene has a length.
A pyrene has a width.
'Shorter than the spathe' is the comparison pattern (docs/odp/09), which maps to decreased length.
A bulbil can have a colour.
A leaf sheath can be convex, but the examples ('fronts convex', 'apex convex') are about the front or apex of the sheath. A rule would need a sheath front/apex part and a check of what is convex.
Roots can be woolly (lanate), as in the Haemodoraceae.
Wrong PATO term. 'mm thick' means thickness (PATO thickness), not depth. Only one flora has it.
Achenes can be globose (spherical).
Perianth lobes can be obovate.
Lobes or their margins can be undulate. The examples are fine.
Areoles on a cactus stem are spaced a distance apart. This is the spacing pattern.
The hardened (indurate) part is the corolla throat, not the whole corolla. A rule would need a throat part, or would have to accept hardness of a region of the corolla.
Sepals can be pale (low saturation colour).
Stems can be pannose (felt-like hair cover).
Capsules can be wrinkled, often when dry.
Pseudoparaphyllia have a shape.
Leaf lobes can be hairy. Some examples are about hairs on the margin, which is acceptable.
An ovary can be adnate to the hypanthium, perianth tube or disc (fused with). This fits the relation pattern.
Pedicels can be farinose (mealy).
A cupule can be tomentose, as in Fagaceae.
Wrong part. The examples describe the ciliate margins of the bud scales, not the bud. The pair belongs to bud scale, not bud.
A keel can be narrow or narrower than another part (decreased width). This fits the comparison pattern.
An epichile apex can be obtuse. The shape is read as that of the epichile.
An indusium can have toothed or denticulate margins.
Achenes can be conical. A few examples describe a cone at the tip, but the pair is fine.
Utricles can be leathery (coriaceous).
A short shoot can be dilated toward the apex.
A moss operculum can be curved.
A pistillate flower has a diameter.
An inflorescence axis (rachis) has a length.
A staminal tube or column has a height.
A branch can be blunt at its distal end.
A rhizome can be perennial (long-lived). It is partly a plant-level trait, but the examples are consistent.
Lateral veins can be prominent or inconspicuous on a leaf face.
A vegetative bud has a length. Some examples are about hairs, but the pair is fine.
Wrong part. 'Cleft 1/3 to 2/3' describes the calyx or corolla, which is cut into lobes. It is not a quality of the flower bud. Only one flora has it.
A stomatal complex has a width in µm. The OCR in the examples is noisy.
Bark can be pale or dark (optical quality values).
Wood (secondary xylem) can be fibrous, soft or hard. The examples are acceptable, though hard or soft would be better mapped to hardness.
A stalk or stipe can be terete.
A perianth can be short or shorter than the bracts (comparison pattern).
A leaf lamina can be angular or pentangular. Some examples are about the lobe apices, but the pair is fine.
A corona lobe can be saccate (pouched), as in Apocynaceae.
A pinna can be curved.
An orchid column (gynostemium) can be clavate.
An inflorescence can be hispidulous.
Pappus elements can have a colour.
